title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ trust in an AI assistant relates to their reliance on AI-generated recommendations during problem-solving, with a particular focus on whether trust is associated with appropriate reliance versus overreliance. The authors frame the problem around the growing use of generative AI in education and the risk that students may accept fluent but incorrect outputs without sufficient evaluation. They ask whether higher trust predicts better calibrated use of AI support, or whether it instead corresponds to weaker discrimination between correct and misleading advice.

To study this, the researchers ran a single-session laboratory experiment with 432 undergraduate students enrolled in computing-related courses at the University of Florida. Participants solved 14 Python output-prediction problems while interacting with an AI chatbot that provided a mix of accurate and intentionally misleading recommendations and explanations. The design used a Wizard-of-Oz approach for the initial responses, with OpenAI API handling follow-up questions. Participants completed pre- and post-task surveys measuring AI literacy, need for cognition, programming self-efficacy, programming literacy, and post-task trust in the assistant.

Results showed that higher trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance, meaning students with greater trust were less likely to accept correct AI advice and reject incorrect advice in a calibrated way. Overreliance on misleading suggestions was common, while underreliance was rare. The trust–reliance relationship was nonlinear but did not reverse within the observed range. AI literacy and need for cognition moderated the association, such that these characteristics were linked to more selective reliance at lower levels of trust, but the negative relationship between trust and appropriate reliance became stronger as trust increased. The authors conclude that educational AI tools should include instructional and system supports that prompt verification and reflective evaluation, such as cognitive forcing functions and justification prompts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental study with a sizable sample and randomized ordering of tasks, but it is not an RCT of an educational intervention in the usual sense and relies on a lab-based Wizard-of-Oz setup plus self-report moderators. It provides credible correlational/experimental evidence about trust and reliance, but not full causal evidence for a learning intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The findings indicate a meaningful negative relationship between trust and appropriate reliance (R2 = .173; r = -0.42) in a programming-learning context, but the study does not test an educational intervention that improves K-12 outcomes. Impact is therefore informative for design and safety, yet the direct educational effect is indirect and the population is higher education rather than K-12.

interventions.use_case: AI chatbot assistant used during programming output-prediction tasks, providing recommendations and explanations with a mix of accurate and intentionally misleading suggestions; follow-up Q&A used OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 in a Wizard-of-Oz setup.

finding.finding_summary: Higher post-task trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance on the AI assistant during Python problem-solving. In the main model, trust negatively predicted appropriate reliance (b = -3.65, SE = 0.39, t(430) = -9.48, p < .001, R2 = .173), indicating less selective acceptance/rejection of AI recommendations as trust increased. The outcome reflects metacognitive judgment and critical evaluation rather than task accuracy alone.
finding.measure: Appropriate reliance on AI recommendations during 14 Python output-prediction problems

finding.finding_summary: Task accuracy was also negatively associated with trust in the AI assistant. Students completed the programming task with mean accuracy of 61.21% (SD = 10.93), and higher trust predicted lower accuracy (r = -0.38, p < .001), consistent with greater acceptance of misleading recommendations in this setting.
finding.measure: Programming task accuracy on 14 Python output-prediction problems

finding.finding_summary: Moderation analyses showed that AI literacy and need for cognition significantly moderated the trust–appropriate reliance relationship, while programming self-efficacy and programming literacy did not. The trust × AI literacy interaction was negative (b = -1.03, p = .014) and the trust × need for cognition interaction was also negative (b = -0.99, p = .040), suggesting these traits supported more selective reliance mainly when trust was lower.
finding.measure: Interaction effects in regression models predicting appropriate reliance from trust and learner characteristics
finding.effect_size: AI literacy interaction b = -1.03; Need for cognition interaction b = -0.99
